Some nouns name a relation,
so they are incomplete without the thing they relate to.
Relational nouns include:

- *cause* (of what?)
- *effect* (of what, on what?)
- *reason* (for what?)
- *result* (of what?)
- *example* (of what?)

When one of these nouns appears without its "of" or "for" phrase,
the reader has to recover the missing object from context,
just as with a pronoun that has no clear referent.
Write the object next to the noun.

::: {#exm-relational-noun}

## Comparing four versions of one sentence

Each version tries to say what usually causes garden-path sentences.

> 1. A common cause in technical writing is a clause that describes a noun
>    but has lost its opening *that* or *that were*.
> 2. In technical writing, a common cause is a clause that describes a noun
>    but has lost its opening *that* or *that were*.
> 3. In technical writing, a common cause of garden-path parsing is a clause
>    that describes a noun but has lost its opening *that* or *that were*.
> 4. A common cause of garden-path sentences in technical writing
>    is a clause that describes a noun
>    but has lost its opening *that* or *that were*.

Versions 1 and 2 never say what the clause causes,
so the reader has to look back to find what "cause" refers to.
Version 3 names the object, "garden-path parsing",
but its fronted phrase delays the subject
(see [Lead with the subject](conciseness.qmd#lead-with-the-subject)),
and "garden-path parsing" introduces a second [term](defining-terms.qmd#def-term)
for the "garden-path sentences" that the section defines.
Version 4 names the object, uses the defined term,
and starts with the subject.

:::

A noun that names a characteristic is relational too:
a bias, a [variance](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#def-variance), an expected squared error, or a risk
is always the bias, variance, error, or risk *of* something.
Name the class of objects the characteristic describes,
such as "the bias of an estimator" or "the expected squared error of a predictor",
every time the characteristic is stated, in a title as well as in prose.
"The bias" alone leaves the reader to guess whether it belongs to
an estimator, a prediction, or a fitted model.

::: {#exm-characteristic-object}

## Naming what a bias describes

> 1. The bias is the average fit minus the true mean function.
> 2. The bias of a prediction at an input $\predvar$ is the average fit at $\predvar$
>    minus the true mean function at $\predvar$.

Version 1 never says what has the bias,
so a reader who meets it as a theorem title cannot tell
whether it is the bias of a coefficient estimate, a prediction, or a whole fitted model.
Version 2 names the class of objects, predictions at an input $\predvar$,
and names $\predvar$ again where the two functions are compared,
instead of pointing back to it with "there".

:::
